rationale: Heritage Crafts defines macramé as textiles made by knotting, describes square knots and half hitches, and identifies wall hangings and knotted jewellery. This supports the prompt and explanation; clearly distinct from patchwork, quilting, and basketry.

rationale: Smithsonian American Art Museum describes basket makers using grasses, trees, vines, and bark, and documents containers made from willow, oak, and bark. Supports materials and basketry identification. Distinct from knotting macramé and textile techniques.

rationale: RSN defines running stitch as equally sized straight surface stitches spaced at intervals to make a line. The sashiko neighbor uses rows of this stitch but asks for the Japanese quilting technique; the candidate asks for the stitch itself, without leaking sashiko as its answer. Distinct from backstitch and split stitch.

RSN defines backstitch by working the visible stitch backwards to produce a continuous solid line. This separates it from running stitch’s gaps and split stitch’s needle-through-thread mechanic; no cue to the sashiko card.

Corning’s stained-glass entry supports colored glass pieces fitted into cames. Companion Came entry says a came is usually lead, rarely another metal, with an H-shaped cross-section, supporting the qualified traditional lead wording and edge-in-groove explanation. Distinct from fusing, blowing, and flameworking.
sourceLocator: Glass Dictionary Definition, lines 83–90; companion Came definition: https://allaboutglass.cmog.org/definition/came

rationale: Corning defines fusing as heating glass pieces in a kiln or furnace until they bond. Directly supports the question and explanation; distinct from cames, blowing through a pipe, and working rods/tubes in flame.
Corning defines blowing as inflating molten glass at the end of a blowpipe and explains the gaffer blows through the tube. Clear distinction from fusing, flameworking, and stained-glass assembly.

Corning defines flameworking as shaping glass rods and tubes after heating them in a flame; it records lamps historically and gas-fueled torches today. Supports the candidate’s typical burner wording and explanation. Distinct from blowpipe inflation and kiln fusing.
sourceLocator: Glass Dictionary Definition, lines 83–87; alternate spelling includes lampwork, lines 88–106
